title: Unique test data and dynamic locators

parts.title: Building a unique value at run time

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 3 - TypeScript - Building a unique value at run time

A **unique value** is a value that no earlier run of the same code has used. This lesson shows the
three pieces that build one: `+` to join text, `Date.now()` for the current time, and
`Math.random()` for a random number.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | The three pieces of TypeScript that build a value that differs on every run. |
| **Goals** | Join text and numbers with `+`, read the current time with `Date.now()`, turn `Math.random()` into a whole number, and combine them into an email. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Week 1 - Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1), for `const`, `console.log`, and template literals. |
| **Tools** | `+`, `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, and `Math.floor()`. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right. The Console tab shows what your code prints. |
| **Key takeaway** | A value built from the current time and a random number differs on every run. |

## 1. Joining text with `+`

Between two pieces of text, `+` joins them into one piece. When one side is a number, `+` turns the
number into text first, and then joins. Nothing is added between the two pieces, so a space appears
only where you write one.

Print a word and a number, joined three ways:

```ts
// Join a word and a number with +, with and without a space.
const prefix = 'learner';
const number = 42;
console.log(prefix + number);
console.log(prefix + ' ' + number);
console.log(prefix + number + '@example.com');
```

**Output**

```output
learner42
learner 42
learner42@example.com
```

**Explanation:** The first line has no space, because `+` adds nothing of its own. The second line
has a space, because `' '` was joined in between. The third line joins three pieces, and the number
in the middle becomes text on the way. This is how the rest of the day builds an email around a
number.

[Week 1 - Day 5 - TypeScript](/learn/w1/d5/p1) introduced the **template literal**, which is text
in backticks with `${}` around each value. Build the same email both ways:

```ts
// Build the same email twice: once with +, once with a template literal.
const prefix = 'learner';
const number = 42;
console.log(prefix + number + '@example.com');
console.log(`${prefix}${number}@example.com`);
```

**Output**

```output
learner42@example.com
learner42@example.com
```

**Explanation:** The two lines print the same text, because the two forms do the same work. `+`
reads well for two or three pieces, and a template literal reads well when the text is long. Either
is fine, and this course uses both.

## 2. `Date.now()`

`Date.now()` returns the current time as a number of milliseconds since the start of 1970. A
**millisecond** is one thousandth of a second, so the number changes one thousand times a second.
Two runs that start a millisecond apart get different numbers.

Print the time, and build an email from it:

```ts
// Read the current time as a number, and build an email from it.
const now = Date.now();
console.log(now);
console.log('learner' + now + '@example.com');
```

**Output**

```output
1790134629851
learner1790134629851@example.com
```

**Explanation:** Your digits differ from these, because your run starts at a different moment. The
number has 13 digits, and it grows by one every millisecond, so a run made later always gets a
larger number. That is what makes it useful as part of a unique value.

## 3. `Math.random()`

`Math.random()` returns a decimal number between 0 and 1, and each call returns a different one. A
decimal is not readable as part of an email, so two more steps turn it into a whole number.
`* 1000000` stretches the range to 0 up to 999999, and `Math.floor()` rounds a number down to the
nearest whole number.

Print two random decimals, then a random whole number:

```ts
// Print two random numbers, then turn one into a whole number with up to six digits.
console.log(Math.random());
console.log(Math.random());
const n = Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000000);
console.log(n);
console.log('learner' + n + '@example.com');
```

**Output**

```output
0.9910865003019883
0.9430810001716421
170624
learner170624@example.com
```

**Explanation:** The two decimals differ although the code that made them is the same, because each
call of `Math.random()` produces a new number. Your digits differ from these on every run. The third
line is a whole number with up to six digits, which reads as part of an email.

## 4. Joining the time and a random number

`Date.now()` alone is enough when one test runs at a time. Playwright runs several tests at once,
and two tests can start in the same millisecond, so both would get the same time. Joining a random
number after the time makes that collision practically impossible. Build the value that the rest of
the day uses:

```ts
// Join the time and a random number, so that two tests started in the same millisecond still differ.
const email = 'learner' + Date.now() + Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000) + '@example.com';
console.log(email);
```

**Output**

```output
learner1790134631368307@example.com
```

**Explanation:** The text joins four pieces: the word `learner`, the 13 digits of the time, up to
three random digits, and `@example.com`. Two tests that start in the same millisecond share the
first two pieces, and the random piece tells them apart.
What does `'learner' + 7` print?

options: `learner 7`, with a space between them
`learner7`, with the number turned into text
An error, because text and a number cannot be added
checkpoint.explanation: `+` turns the number into text and joins the two pieces with nothing between them. A space appears only where you write one, so the first option would need `' '` joined in the middle.

blocks.text: Two tests start in the same millisecond, and each calls `Date.now()`. What happens?

options: Both tests get the same number.
The second test gets the number plus one.
The second test waits until the next millisecond.
checkpoint.explanation: `Date.now()` reads the clock, and the clock shows the same millisecond to both tests. It does not count calls or wait, which is why the lesson joins a random number after the time.

blocks.text: What does `Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000000)` return?

options: A whole number from 0 to 999999
A decimal between 0 and 1
A whole number from 1 to 1000000
checkpoint.explanation: `Math.random()` gives a decimal from 0 up to, but not including, 1. Multiplying by 1000000 stretches it to below 1000000, and `Math.floor()` rounds down, so the largest result is 999999 and the smallest is 0.

blocks.text:
- `+` joins text, and turns a number into text on the way. A template literal does the same work with `${}`.
- `Date.now()` returns the current time in milliseconds, so a later run always gets a larger number.
- `Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000000)` returns a random whole number with up to six digits.
- The time joined with a random number gives a value that differs on every run, even for two tests that start in the same millisecond.

## What's next

[Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d3/p2) types a value built this way into the registration form, and shows
why a locator cannot find the field by that value.

parts.title: Unique test data and dynamic locators

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 3 - Fundamentals - Unique test data and dynamic locators

**Test data** is the set of values that a test types into an application, such as a name, an email,
or a phone number. This lesson builds test data that differs on every run, and builds a locator from
a value chosen at run time.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Test data that differs on every run, and a locator built from a value at run time. |
| **Goals** | Fill the registration form with a unique email, explain the difference between an attribute and a property, and select a radio button through a dynamic locator. |
| **Prerequisites** | [TypeScript](/learn/w2/d3/p1) for building the value, and [Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d2/p2) for `page.locator()` with CSS and XPath. |
| **Tools** | `page.locator()`, `getAttribute()`, `inputValue()`, `count()`, `check()`, `toHaveValue`, and `toBeChecked`. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right for the examples, then your own project for the spec file. Both use the registration form at `demo.automationtesting.in`. |
| **Key takeaway** | An attribute is written in the markup, and a property is what the element holds now, so a typed value can be read back but not located. |

## Why a test needs a new email on every run

Many applications refuse a second sign-up with an email they have already seen. A test that types
the same email every time passes on its first run, and fails on every later run, because the
application reports that the email is taken. The test is correct, the application is correct, and
the failure comes from the data. The registration form at
`https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html` accepts any email, so nothing fails here. The
lesson builds the habit on this form, where a mistake costs nothing.

variation.prompt: Build a unique first name the same way, such as 'Learner' + Date.now(), and print it. Fill it into the First Name box with page.getByPlaceholder('First Name'), and show a screenshot.

blocks.text:
## Best practices

- Build the unique value once, store it in a `const`, and use that `const` to fill and to assert, so
  both steps use the same text.
- Print the value with `console.log`, so a failed run tells you which data it used.
- Match `@value` in an XPath only against a value written in the markup, such as a radio button's.
- Read what a field holds with `inputValue()`, or check it with `toHaveValue`, never with an XPath.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Built the email inside `fill()` and again inside `toHaveValue()` | The assertion fails, because each call built a different email | Build the email once, in a `const`, and use it in both places. |
| Looked for a typed value with `//input[@value='...']` | The locator finds nothing, and an action on it times out | Use the locator that filled the field, and read it with `inputValue()`. |
| Typed the same email on every run of a sign-up test | The first run passes, and later runs report that the email is taken | Build the email from `Date.now()` and `Math.random()`. |
| Wrote the template literal in single quotes | The text `${gender}` appears in the locator as it is, and nothing matches | Put the text in backticks, not in single quotes. |
You fill the email box with `learner1@example.com`. Which call gives that text back?

options: `emailBox.getAttribute('value')`
`emailBox.inputValue()`
`page.locator("//input[@value='learner1@example.com']")`
checkpoint.explanation: Typing changes the property, and `inputValue()` reads the property. `getAttribute('value')` reads the markup, where nothing was written, so it returns `null`, and the XPath finds no element for the same reason.

blocks.text: Why does `//input[@value='FeMale']` find the gender radio button?

options: Its `value` is written in the page's markup.
Playwright writes the value into the markup when it selects a radio button.
A radio button keeps a `value` attribute and no property.
checkpoint.explanation: The radio button's `value` was in the HTML before any code ran, so `@value` matches it. Selecting a radio button changes which one is checked, and writes nothing into the markup.

blocks.text: What makes a locator dynamic?

options: Its text is built from a value at run time.
It keeps retrying until the element appears on the page.
It matches several elements instead of only one.
checkpoint.explanation: A dynamic locator is written as a template literal with a value inside `${}`, so its text is decided while the test runs. Every Playwright locator retries, so retrying is not what sets a dynamic locator apart.

blocks.text:
- Test data that differs on every run keeps a sign-up test passing on its second run and on every run after it.
- An **attribute** is written in the markup and does not change when you type. A **property** is what the element holds now.
- A typed value can be read with `inputValue()` or checked with `toHaveValue`, but an XPath with `@value` cannot find it.
- A dynamic locator is built at run time with a template literal, and it works when the value it contains is in the markup.

## What's next

[Implementation](/learn/w2/d3/p3) moves the line that builds the email into a function in your helper
file, so that every test can call it.

parts.title: A helper that returns a unique email

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 3 - Implementation - A helper that returns a unique email

A **helper** is a function that several tests call, kept in a file of its own. This lesson adds one
to the helper file from [Day 1 - Implementation](/learn/w2/d1/p3), so that no test repeats the line
that builds an email.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | A `uniqueEmail()` helper in `registration-helpers.ts`, so that no test repeats the line that builds an email. |
| **Goals** | Add an exported function with a return type to the helper file, and use it from two tests that each get their own email. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d3/p2), where you built the email inside a test, and [Day 1 - Implementation](/learn/w2/d1/p3), where `registration-helpers.ts` was created. |
| **Tools** | `export`, a `: string` return type, and `import` from `./registration-helpers`. |
| **Environment** | VS Code and its integrated terminal, in your project folder. |
| **Key takeaway** | A helper builds the value inside its function body, so every call returns a new one. |

## The problem with the Fundamentals version

The test in [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d3/p2) builds its email with
`'learner' + Date.now() + '@example.com'`. Every test that registers a user needs the same line. If
ten tests each contain it, and the application starts to reject long emails, you change ten lines.
If the line is in one function, you change one line, and every test gets the change.

## Why it is shaped this way

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| The email is built inside the function, not in a `const` at the top of the file | A `const` at the top of the file is computed once, when the file loads, so every test would get the same email. |
| The function takes no parameters | Every caller wants the same kind of value, so there is nothing to pass in. |
| The function returns the email instead of filling the field | The test needs the email twice, to fill and to assert, so the function hands the value back and the test decides what to do with it. |
| `fillRegistrationForm` takes the email as a parameter | The helper that fills the form does not decide what the email is, so a test can pass a unique one or a fixed one. |

## What a reviewer looks for

- The line that builds an email appears once, in `registration-helpers.ts`, and in no spec file.
- Each test calls `uniqueEmail()` once, stores the result in a `const`, and uses that `const` for
  both the fill and the assertion.
- The helper file contains no `test()`, and its name has no `.spec`, so Playwright never runs it as
  a test file.
Two tests in the same file each call `uniqueEmail()`. Do they get the same email?

options: Yes, because the file is loaded once.
No, because the body runs again on each call.
Yes, unless the tests run in different workers.
checkpoint.explanation: The line that builds the email is inside the function, so every call runs it again and reads a new time and a new random number. Loading the file once defines the function, and does not run it.

blocks.text: Why is the email built inside `uniqueEmail()` instead of in a `const` at the top of the helper file?

options: A `const` at the top of the file is computed once and shared.
A `const` cannot be exported to a spec file.
A `const` cannot hold text that was built with `+` and `Date.now()`.
checkpoint.explanation: A `const` at the top of a file is computed once, when the file loads, so every test that imports it would get the same email. That is the collision the helper exists to prevent. A `const` can be exported, and it can hold any text.

blocks.text: Why does the test store the result of `uniqueEmail()` in a `const` before it fills the form?

options: So the fill and the assertion use the same email.
Because `fillRegistrationForm` accepts only a `const`, never a call.
Because a function's result cannot be passed to another function.
checkpoint.explanation: The test needs the email twice, to fill the box and to check it. A second call of `uniqueEmail()` would build a different email, and the assertion would compare the box with an email that was never typed.

blocks.text:
- `uniqueEmail()` lives in `registration-helpers.ts`, and every test imports it instead of repeating the line.
- The value is built inside the function body, so each call returns a new email.
- A test calls the helper once, stores the result in a `const`, and uses it for both the fill and the assertion.

## What's next

[Practice](/learn/w2/d3/p4) has you print unique emails in the editor, register with
`uniqueEmail()`, and write a second helper for a phone number.

# Week 2 - Day 3 - Practice - Unique data and dynamic locators

These three problems use the value building from [TypeScript](/learn/w2/d3/p1), the attribute and
property distinction from [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d3/p2), and the helper from
[Implementation](/learn/w2/d3/p3). The first problem runs in the editor, and the other two run in
your own project.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Three problems about unique test data, from Beginner level to Advanced. |
| **Prerequisites** | [TypeScript](/learn/w2/d3/p1) for building the value, [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d3/p2) for the form, and [Implementation](/learn/w2/d3/p3) for the helper file. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right for the first problem, and your own project for the other two. |

## How to answer

The problems run from Beginner to Advanced. Select **Start this in the editor** to open a template
for a problem, and write your answer on the lines that start with `//`. Select **Reveal solution**
to compare it with a model answer.

## When you are done

You can build a value that no earlier run has used, keep it in a `const` so that the fill and the
assertion agree, and build a locator from a value chosen at run time.
[Day 4 - Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d4/p2) continues from here.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Three unique emails, each built with `Date.now()` and `Math.random()` as in
[TypeScript](/learn/w2/d3/p1), and each printed with `console.log`. Below them, write a comment
that explains why the three emails differ.

**Where.** In the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** The Console tab shows three emails, and no two of them are the
same.

**What to build.** A test that registers with `uniqueEmail()` and checks the email box. In the
`tests` folder, create `practice-unique.spec.ts`, with one test that calls `uniqueEmail()`, stores
the result in a `const`, passes it to `fillRegistrationForm`, and asserts the email box with
`toHaveValue`. Print the email with `console.log`. Then run the test twice.

**Where.** In VS Code and its integrated terminal. Copy your test and the two printed emails into
the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** Both runs report `1 passed`, and the two printed emails differ.

**Hint.** Call `uniqueEmail()` once. A second call gives a different email, and the assertion would
compare the box with an email that was never typed.

**What to build.** A second helper, `uniquePhone()`, and a test that uses it. In
`tests/registration-helpers.ts`, add an exported function `uniquePhone()` that returns ten digits as
text. Build it with `String(Math.floor(Math.random() * 10000000000)).padStart(10, '0')`. `String()`
turns a number into text, and `padStart(10, '0')` adds `0` at the front until the text is ten
characters long. Then create `practice-phone.spec.ts`, with one test that checks the phone number
with `expect(phone.length).toBe(10)`, fills the form, fills the **Phone** box
(`input[type='tel']`) with the phone number, and asserts the box with `toHaveValue`.

**Where.** In VS Code and its integrated terminal. Copy the new function and your test into the
editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** The test reports `1 passed`, and the printed phone number has ten
digits, even when it starts with `0`.

**Hint.** `phone.length` is the number of characters in the text. `Math.random() * 10000000000`
sometimes gives a number with fewer than ten digits, and `padStart` fills the missing places.
